units.sourceHTML: Configuring the VM
units.originalInnerHTML: Configuring the VM

units.sourceHTML:
When you create a Wren VM, you tweak it by passing in a pointer to a
WrenConfiguration structure. Since Wren has no global state, you can configure
each VM differently if your application happens to run multiple.

When you create a Wren VM, you tweak it by passing in a pointer to a
WrenConfiguration structure. Since Wren has no global state, you can configure
each VM differently if your application happens to run multiple.

units.sourceHTML: Binding #
units.originalInnerHTML: Binding #

units.sourceHTML:
The VM is isolated from the outside world. These callbacks let the VM request
access to imported code and foreign functionality.
units.originalInnerHTML:
The VM is isolated from the outside world. These callbacks let the VM request
access to imported code and foreign functionality.

units.sourceHTML: ⟦CODE0⟧ #
units.originalInnerHTML: loadModuleFn #

units.sourceHTML:
This is the callback Wren uses to load an imported module. The VM itself does
not know how to talk to the file system, so when an ⟦CODE0⟧ statement is
executed, it relies on the host application to locate and read the source code
for a module.
units.originalInnerHTML: This is the callback Wren uses to load an imported module. The VM itself does not know how to talk to the file system, so when an import statement is executed, it relies on the host application to locate and read the source code for a module.

units.sourceHTML: The signature of this function is:
units.originalInnerHTML: The signature of this function is:

units.sourceHTML:
When a module is imported, Wren calls this and passes in the module’s name. The
host should return the source code for that module in a ⟦CODE0⟧ struct.
units.originalInnerHTML: When a module is imported, Wren calls this and passes in the module’s name. The host should return the source code for that module in a WrenLoadModuleResult struct.

units.sourceHTML:
The module loader is only be called once for any given module name. Wren caches
the result internally so subsequent imports of the same module use the
previously loaded code.
units.originalInnerHTML:
The module loader is only be called once for any given module name. Wren caches
the result internally so subsequent imports of the same module use the
previously loaded code.

units.sourceHTML:
If your host application isn’t able to load a module with some name, it should
make sure the ⟦CODE0⟧ value is ⟦CODE1⟧ when returned. Wren will then report that as a runtime error.
units.originalInnerHTML: If your host application isn’t able to load a module with some name, it should make sure the source value is NULL when returned. Wren will then report that as a runtime error.

units.sourceHTML:
If you don’t use any ⟦CODE0⟧ statements, you can leave the ⟦CODE1⟧ field in
the configuration set to ⟦CODE2⟧ (the default).
units.originalInnerHTML: If you don’t use any import statements, you can leave the loadModuleFn field in the configuration set to NULL (the default).

units.sourceHTML:
Additionally, the ⟦CODE0⟧ allows us to add a callback for when Wren is 
done with the ⟦CODE1⟧, so we can free the memory if needed.
units.originalInnerHTML: Additionally, the WrenLoadModuleResult allows us to add a callback for when Wren is done with the source, so we can free the memory if needed.

outside world and lets you do rudimentary “printf debugging”. Its signature is:

units.originalInnerHTML: errorFn #

units.sourceHTML:
Wren uses this callback to report compile time and runtime errors. Its signature

units.sourceHTML: The ⟦CODE0⟧ parameter is one of:

units.sourceHTML:
When a compile error occurs, ⟦CODE0⟧ is called once with type
⟦CODE1⟧, the name of the module and line where the error occurs,
and the error message.
units.originalInnerHTML: When a compile error occurs, errorFn is called once with type WREN_ERROR_COMPILE, the name of the module and line where the error occurs, and the error message.

units.sourceHTML:
Runtime errors include stack traces. To handle this, Wren first calls ⟦CODE0⟧
with ⟦CODE1⟧, no module or line, and the runtime error’s message.
After that, it calls ⟦CODE2⟧ again using type ⟦CODE3⟧, once
for each line in the stack trace. Each of those calls has the module and line
where the method or function is defined and ⟦CODE4⟧ is the name of the method
or function.
units.originalInnerHTML: Runtime errors include stack traces. To handle this, Wren first calls errorFn with WREN_ERROR_RUNTIME, no module or line, and the runtime error’s message. After that, it calls errorFn again using type WREN_ERROR_STACK_TRACE, once for each line in the stack trace. Each of those calls has the module and line where the method or function is defined and message is the name of the method or function.

units.sourceHTML: If you leave this ⟦CODE0⟧, Wren does not report any errors.
units.originalInnerHTML: If you leave this NULL, Wren does not report any errors.

units.sourceHTML: Memory Management #
units.originalInnerHTML: Memory Management #

units.sourceHTML: These fields control how the VM allocates and manages memory.
units.originalInnerHTML: These fields control how the VM allocates and manages memory.

units.sourceHTML: ⟦CODE0⟧ #
units.originalInnerHTML: reallocateFn #

units.sourceHTML: This lets you provide a custom memory allocation function. Its signature is:
units.originalInnerHTML: This lets you provide a custom memory allocation function. Its signature is:

units.sourceHTML:
Wren uses this one function to allocate, grow, shrink, and deallocate memory.
When called, ⟦CODE0⟧ is the existing pointer to the block of memory if an
allocation is being changed or freed. If Wren is requesting new memory, then
⟦CODE1⟧ is ⟦CODE2⟧.
units.originalInnerHTML: Wren uses this one function to allocate, grow, shrink, and deallocate memory. When called, memory is the existing pointer to the block of memory if an allocation is being changed or freed. If Wren is requesting new memory, then memory is NULL.

units.sourceHTML:
⟦CODE0⟧ is the number of bytes of memory being requested. If memory is being
freed, this is zero. Your callback should allocate the proper amount of memory
and return it.
units.originalInnerHTML: newSize is the number of bytes of memory being requested. If memory is being freed, this is zero. Your callback should allocate the proper amount of memory and return it.

units.sourceHTML:
If you don’t provide a custom allocator, the VM uses a default one that relies
on ⟦CODE0⟧ and ⟦CODE1⟧.
units.originalInnerHTML: If you don’t provide a custom allocator, the VM uses a default one that relies on realloc and free.

units.sourceHTML: ⟦CODE0⟧ #
units.originalInnerHTML: initialHeapSize #

units.sourceHTML:
This defines the total number of bytes of memory the VM will allocate before
triggering the first garbage collection. Setting this to a smaller number
reduces the amount of memory Wren will have allocated at one time, but causes it
to collect garbage more frequently.
units.originalInnerHTML:
This defines the total number of bytes of memory the VM will allocate before
triggering the first garbage collection. Setting this to a smaller number
reduces the amount of memory Wren will have allocated at one time, but causes it
to collect garbage more frequently.

units.sourceHTML: If you set this to zero, Wren uses a default size of 10MB.
units.originalInnerHTML: If you set this to zero, Wren uses a default size of 10MB.

units.sourceHTML: ⟦CODE0⟧ #
units.originalInnerHTML: minHeapSize #

units.sourceHTML: After a garbage collection occurs, the threshold for the next collection is determined based on the number of bytes remaining in use. This allows Wren to grow or shrink its memory usage automatically based on how much memory is actually needed.
units.originalInnerHTML: After a garbage collection occurs, the threshold for the next collection is determined based on the number of bytes remaining in use. This allows Wren to grow or shrink its memory usage automatically based on how much memory is actually needed.

units.sourceHTML: This can be used to ensure that the heap does not get too small, which can in turn lead to a large number of collections afterwards as the heap grows back to a usable size.
units.originalInnerHTML: This can be used to ensure that the heap does not get too small, which can in turn lead to a large number of collections afterwards as the heap grows back to a usable size.

units.sourceHTML: If zero, this defaults to 1MB.
units.originalInnerHTML: If zero, this defaults to 1MB.

units.sourceHTML: ⟦CODE0⟧ #
units.originalInnerHTML: heapGrowthPercent #

units.sourceHTML:
Wren tunes the rate of garbage collection based on how much memory is still in
use after a collection. This number controls that. It determines the amount of
additional memory Wren will use after a collection, as a percentage of the
current heap size.
units.originalInnerHTML:
Wren tunes the rate of garbage collection based on how much memory is still in
use after a collection. This number controls that. It determines the amount of
additional memory Wren will use after a collection, as a percentage of the
current heap size.

units.sourceHTML:
For example, say that this is 50. After a garbage collection, there are 400
bytes of memory still in use. That means the next collection will be triggered
after a total of 600 bytes are allocated (including the 400 already in use.)
units.originalInnerHTML:
For example, say that this is 50. After a garbage collection, there are 400
bytes of memory still in use. That means the next collection will be triggered
after a total of 600 bytes are allocated (including the 400 already in use.)

units.sourceHTML:
Setting this to a smaller number wastes less memory, but triggers more
frequent garbage collections.
units.originalInnerHTML:
Setting this to a smaller number wastes less memory, but triggers more
frequent garbage collections.

units.sourceHTML: If set to zero, the VM uses a default of 50.
units.originalInnerHTML: If set to zero, the VM uses a default of 50.
